b: The associations are seeking targeted support for logging and log-hauling businesses excluded from the $8bn Harvest Fuel Relief programme, citing rising diesel costs and pressure on rural operations.
Rising fuel costs are putting pressure on logging and log-hauling businesses across rural US communities (Image: Unsplash)

A coalition of 43 US forestry associations has called on the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to extend diesel fuel assistance to logging and log-hauling businesses excluded from its recently announced $8bn Harvest Fuel Relief programme.

Coordinated by the Forest Resources Association (FRA), the coalition submitted a joint letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins on 27 Oct, urging the department to introduce targeted support for timber harvesters and hauliers.

The associations cited findings from FRA Technical Release 26-TR-24, which highlighted the impact of rising fuel expenditure and per-mile transportation costs on contractors. The increased costs are putting pressure on businesses and forcing some to idle equipment in rural communities. The estimates do not include diesel consumed by in-woods harvesting or processing equipment.

The letter referred to the Pandemic Assistance for Timber Harvesters and Haulers (PATHH) programme as a precedent for targeted support. The coalition urged the USDA to recognise timber harvesters and hauliers as essential, diesel-dependent partners in the forest products supply chain and establish a relief initiative to help maintain the country’s wood supply.

“Logging and timber-hauling businesses are the backbone of the forest products supply chain, yet they are currently absorbing unsustainable, multi-thousand-dollar weekly spikes in diesel costs with zero federal support,” said Tim O’Hara, president and CEO of the FRA.
“While we fully support assistance for agricultural producers, we urge the USDA to recognise that forestry contractors face the exact same fuel volatility and operational pressures,” he said.
